Key ideas

The properties of waves

Definitions

Medium: a substance or material that can carry the vibrations of a wave
Transverse wave: a wave in which vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel
Longitudinal wave: a wave in which vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel
Compression: in longitudinal waves, a region where particles are most closely spaced
Rarefaction: in waves, a region where particles are most spread out

Formulas

The wave equation
λ=vf=vT\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = vTλ=fv​=vT
λ\lambdaλWavelength of the wave (m\mathrm{m}m)vvvSpeed of the wave (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}ms−1)fffFrequency of the wave (Hz\mathrm{Hz}Hz)TTTPeriod of the wave (s\mathrm{s}s)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 1A glossary and formula boxes3
1A

Key ideas

The properties of waves

Definitions

Amplitude, A: a measure of the size of vibrations in a wave as the maximum distance a point in the wave vibrates away from the neutral position; generally measured in metres (m)
Frequency, f: the number of wavelengths of a wave that pass a fixed point in a second; measured in hertz (Hz)
Wavelength, λ: the distance between repeated parts of a wave shape; measured in metres (m)
Period, T: the time it takes for a wave to move one wavelength in the direction of travel; measured in seconds (s)

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 1A glossary and formula boxes4
1A

New knowledgeThe nature of waves

The properties of waves

The source of all waves is a vibration of some kind.

Mechanical waves vibrate particles of a medium.

The vibrations then spread though the medium.

Non-mechanical waves, such as light waves, do not require a medium.

Figure 1A–1 Transverse wave in a slinky spring
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 65
1A

New knowledgeThe nature of waves

The properties of waves

Their vibrations are electrical and magnetic, and they can travel through both transparent materials and a vacuum, such as the space between the Sun and Earth.

You can recognise waves by their vibrations and the fact that they transfer energy without transferring matter.

A good example of a simple mechanical wave can be seen when a slinky spring is shaken at a steady rate, as shown in Figure 1A–1.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 66
1A

New knowledgeThe nature of waves (transverse and longitudinal)

The properties of waves

If you look carefully at the movement of the spring, you will notice that although the wave moves to the left, the individual coils of the spring do not move left (or right); they just vibrate up and down.

Waves like this are called transverse waves.

Another everyday example of transverse waves are water waves, such as ocean swells or ripples in a pond where the water particles move more or less up and down as the wave moves along.

There are other kinds of waves where the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel of the wave; these are called longitudinal waves.

Figure 1A–2 Longitudinal wave in a slinky spring
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 67
1A

New knowledgeThe nature of waves (transverse and longitudinal)

The properties of waves

These can also be shown by shaking a slinky parallel to its length.

Sound waves are also examples of this kind of wave.

You can set up a longitudinal wave in a slinky spring as shown in Figure 1A–2.

The vibrations create regions of compression, where the particles of the slinky are more closely spaced, and rarefactions, where the particles are more spread out.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 68
1A

New knowledgeThe nature of waves (transverse and longitudinal)

The properties of waves

In the example of the slinky spring waves, the energy input from the shaking hand at one end appears as energy at the other end of the spring.

However, the particles of the slinky spring simply vibrate in the one place to and fro and do not travel from one end of the spring to the other end, but the vibrations do.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 69
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves

The properties of waves

The key terms describing waves are amplitude, frequency, wavelength, period and speed.

Figure 1A–3 shows these terms applied to a transverse wave in a slinky spring.

Amplitude, AAA, is a measure of the size of the wave vibrations; it is the maximum displacement from the neutral (mid-point) position.

It is generally measured in metres.

Figure 1A–3 Idealised sinusoidal transverse wave
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 710
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves

The properties of waves

Wavelength, λ\lambdaλ, is the distance between repeated parts of the wave shape.

It is also measured in metres.

Speed, vvv, is the speed of the wave as it moves.

It is different from the transverse speed of the particles of the medium.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 711
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves

The properties of waves

It is measured in metres per second (m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1).

The speed of a wave is determined by the properties of the medium through which it travels.

Period, TTT, is the time for the wave shape to move one wavelength in the direction of travel.

It is measured in seconds.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 712
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves

The properties of waves

Frequency, fff, is equal to the number of wave shapes that pass a point every second.

It is equal to 1T\frac{1}{T}T1​ and is measured in hertz (Hz).

The frequency of a wave is only determined by the source that generates it and does not depend on the nature of medium.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 713
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves (the wave equation)

The properties of waves

The wavelength, λ\lambdaλ, of a wave depends only on the nature of the medium through which the wave moves and is related to the speed, vvv, and frequency, fff, of the wave.

If a wave is travelling at a speed of vvv m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1, then every second the wave will travel a distance of vvv m from a fixed point.

At the same time, if the frequency of the wave is fff Hz, then every second, fff wave shapes go past the same fixed point.

Hence, in each second the wave travels a distance vvv m from a fixed point and fff wave shapes go past the same point, so in symbols the length of each wave shape is: [Formula 1A–1] This equation shows the relationship between wavelength, frequency, speed and period and applies to all types of waves.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 714
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves (the wave equation)

The properties of waves

The frequency of a wave depends only on the source of the wave and not on the medium, whereas the speed of the wave depends on the nature of the medium.

Using this relationship, since frequency is constant between media, the wavelength must also depend on the nature of the medium to make up for changes in the speed of the wave in different media.

For example, if a wave increases speed going from one medium to another, then from Formula 1A–1 the wavelength must also increase in the medium by the same amount since fff does not change between media.

This shows that while fff does not depend on the medium, wavelength and the speed of the wave do depend on the medium.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 715
1A

New knowledgeDescribing waves (the wave equation)

The properties of waves

Usually Formula 1A–1 will be written in the form v=fλv = f\lambdav=fλ and is referred to as the wave equation.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 1, p. 716

We doPeriod and frequency of a wave

The properties of waves
Find the period and frequency of a water wave of wavelength 8.0 m and speed 5.0 m s−1\text{m s}^{-1}m s−1.
Key idea · The wave equationλ=vf=vT\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = vTλ=fv​=vT

Working

Using λ=vf\lambda = \frac{v}{f}λ=fv​ to find the frequency and making fff the subject gives:
f=vλf = \frac{v}{\lambda}f=λv​
=5.08.0= \frac{5.0}{8.0}=8.05.0​
=0.625 Hz= 0.625\ \text{Hz}=0.625 Hz
Using the definition of fff to find the period gives:
T=1fT = \frac{1}{f}T=f1​
=10.625= \frac{1}{0.625}=0.6251​
=1.6 s= 1.6\ \text{s}=1.6 s
f=0.625f = 0.625f=0.625 Hz, T=1.6T = 1.6T=1.6 s

Do now

The properties of waves
Check-in set 1 · Q1 · 1A
What is the difference between a transverse and a longitudinal wave?
In a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of the wave's motion; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel.
Check-in set 1 · Q2 · 1A
What is the difference between a mechanical and a non-mechanical wave?
A mechanical wave requires a medium of matter for its transmission; a non-mechanical wave does not require a medium for its transmission.
Check-in set 1 · Q3 · 1A
How does a mechanical wave motion transfer energy from one place to another?
Wave motion transfers energy by transferring vibrations rather than any material of the medium.
